description: NISAR radar satellites can detect ground changes through clouds, day or night, but the data is too complex for most people to use. We're building a simple web tool that compares radar scenes over time and turns them into clear map alerts: where land is sinking, where flooding has spread, where the surface is changing. We're starting with Egypt's Nile Delta. Planners, farmers and insurers get plain-language warnings instead of raw files, so they can act early.
summary: Beneath the Sand uses NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar to reveal river channels buried under the Sahara’s dry sand, which are invisible in ordinary photos. We processed real NISAR data covering about 12,000 km² near the Egypt–Sudan border and traced candidate channels from the radar. An interactive map shows them beside known archaeological sites and published buried rivers, such as the Bir Safsaf radar rivers. A machine-learning model and crowd tagging help separate real channels from rock cracks, dunes and tracks. The result becomes ranked field survey targets that archaeology teams can take into the desert. Ancient rivers mark where early humans lived and travelled, yet no open map of them exists, and AI research lacks labeled data. We aim to release our labels openly. Our results are candidates for expert verification, not discoveries.
details:
What it does and how it works
Beneath the Sand turns NISAR radar into a map of buried river channels. L-band radar can pass through dry sand and return echoes from the layers below, so channels that look like plain desert on the surface appear as lines and valleys in the radar. Our Python pipeline downloads NISAR GCOV data (HH and HV polarizations) from NASA, converts it to decibels and combines HH, HV and their difference. It then traces ridge and valley features and cuts the mosaic into 5 km patches. The web app opens with a guided tour that reveals the hidden rivers. Its live map shows traced channels, buried valleys and 17 known places, including published buried rivers used to check the radar. Users can also add radar for new areas with their own free NASA Earthdata login. A U-Net model suggests channels, a trust model weights tagger reliability, and top candidates are meant to export as survey plans (KML, GPX, CSV) for archaeologists.

Benefits
Desert fieldwork is expensive, slow and risky, and the Sahara is about 9 million km². Radar candidates let teams spend limited time on the most promising places. NASA’s data is free, so any team with a laptop can repeat the work. Our labeled patches also address the shortage of labeled data that holds back AI mapping of buried rivers.

Intended impact
We want to give archaeologists and researchers a practical starting point: an open map of candidate channels near known sites, ranked and ready to survey. Because NISAR re-scans the same areas every 12 days, the approach can grow from one region to the whole Sahara. Crowd tagging also invites the public to take part in discovery. We present every result as a candidate to verify on the ground.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Frontend: React, Vite, TypeScript, MapLibre GL
  • Backend: Express, Prisma, PostgreSQL with PostGIS, Docker Compose
  • Data and AI: Python (earthaccess, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, pyproj, rasterio, Pillow, Matplotlib), PyTorch U-Net
  • Data source: NISAR L2 GCOV from NASA Earthdata (ASF DAAC)
  • Hardware: team laptops; the model trains in about 1.5 minutes on an RTX 3050 laptop GPU

Creativity
Most teams will use NISAR to show change over time. We use it as a time machine, to see what the desert hid thousands of years ago. The experience is built around a reveal: empty sand, then radar, then rivers. The AI suggestion is hidden until a person answers, so tagging stays independent, and a trust model filters careless or malicious tags. The output is a field-ready survey plan rather than just a map.

Factors we considered

  • False positives: rock cracks, dunes, straight tracks and radar speckle can look like channels, so we check against published buried rivers and use gold-standard patches.
  • Honesty: we call results candidates and cite earlier fieldwork rather than claim discoveries.
  • Data limits: NISAR’s public record is short, and radar penetration depends on dry sand.
  • Reliability: data is pre-downloaded so the demo works on slow venue internet.
  • Openness: labels and patches are designed to be shared.
